### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Polikoff and colleagues report a fall-2023 wave of the Understanding America Study (a probability-based, address-sampled panel; 3,905 completers, fielded September 19–October 29, 2023) in which adults rated whether 18 concrete race-related classroom topics are appropriate, separately for elementary and high school, alongside six general attitude items. The descriptive core is solid and is what the paper should be cited for: every one of the 18 topics draws majority support (56–92%) for high school while only 5 of 18 do for elementary (Figure 1, p.6); the Democrat–Republican difference on the IRT support scale is 1.03 theta points, about 1.1 SD (Table 3, Model 1, p.9); and bivariate county and state partisanship gaps (county strong Republican −0.51) collapse to near zero (−0.09) once individual party identification enters (Model 8), so place-based differences in opinion are mostly differences in who lives there. Every count the writing reviewer checked in the Results narrative matched the bar charts, and the reproducibility reviewer found that the Figure 1 values and Table 1 match the publicly posted UAS topline to the percentage point. The title's question — what *explains* the partisan gap — is answered far less securely. The "explanation" is sequential OLS with one attitude item added at a time; the "more than half" and "approximately 30% to 40%" shares on p.8 hold only against the bivariate Model 1, while the "about 25%" shares on p.10 hold only against Model 8, so no single baseline reproduces the text; Models 9–13 are estimated on roughly half the sample (N = 1,727–1,827 versus 3,892) with no explanation and no like-for-like baseline; the Discussion's "about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) corresponds to no model in Table 3, where the two items never appear together; and the strongest "explanator" ("Children should learn about the ways White people have been racist historically in the U.S. even if that makes them feel guilty") is close to being another support item, so its absorbing the partisan coefficient says little about mechanism and does not isolate "concern about White students feeling guilty" as the abstract puts it. Add that the novelty claims are oversold (the authors' own 2024 project report had already published the high-school majorities, an IRT scale, and the guilt conjecture; the "opt-in panel" criticism on p.3 does not fit the Pew and Monmouth polls it is aimed at; the education-politics literature on partisan sorting is absent), that the sample bookkeeping on p.3 does not reconcile with the Ns in Table 3, and that the article carries no data statement, code, software, weighting, or standard-error information, and the right posture is: rely on Figures 1–2 and the Model 1 versus Model 8 comparison, always quote the fielding date, and treat the decomposition percentages, the "deep-red states" framing, and the media and policy narrative of the Discussion as hypotheses the data motivate rather than findings they establish.

#### Key Strengths

- A genuinely finer-grained instrument than anything in the prior polling: 18 behaviorally specific topics (full wording in Table 2, p.5), pretested in two rounds of cognitive interviews, asked separately for Grades K–5 and 9–12, with support ranging from 18% to 92% across items (Figure 1, p.6). The elementary/high-school contrast — 5 of 18 majorities versus 18 of 18 — is the paper's most useful new fact and is directly visible in the exhibit.
- A probability-based panel with survey weights, a stated field period, and Rao-Scott-adjusted tests for the group comparisons (pp.3, 6). For national item-level percentages this is about as good as online survey data get, and the descriptive exhibits reproduce against the public UAS topline.
- The geography decomposition is clean and citable: county and state partisanship gaps that are large bivariately (Models 3–4) are almost entirely absorbed by individual party identification (Model 8), while the partisan coefficients themselves barely move when demographics are added (−1.03 to −0.94; −0.61 to −0.52). Place is mostly composition.
- The Results narrative on pp.6–7 is faithful to Figures 1 and 2. Every count the writing reviewer checked (five elementary majorities, eight items below one-third, majority high-school support for all 18, "four of the top five," 15 of 18 majorities in strong-Republican states) matches the printed bar values.
- The authors state plainly that the attitude regressions are not causal (p.8) and that the findings are descriptive (p.10), and Table 3 reports N, R², df, F, and RMSE for all 14 models, which is what let the reviewers audit it.

#### Key Concerns

- The "share of the partisan gap explained" figures cannot be reproduced against any single baseline. Against Model 8 (Republican −0.94, Neither −0.52), the guilt item (Model 13: −0.48, −0.30) accounts for 49% and 42%, not "more than half"; the "more than half" holds only against the uncontrolled Model 1 (53%, 51%). The "about 25%" shares for Models 10 and 14 hold only against Model 8 (19–25%), not Model 1 (28–36%). The text also never says which baseline it used.
- Models 9–13 use roughly half the sample (N = 1,727–1,827 versus 3,892 in Model 8 and 3,818 in Model 14; Table 3, p.9) and the text never says why. Model 9, whose added item is null (−0.04), already moves the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.88, so part of every "explained" share is sample change. No Model 8 baseline on the reduced sample is reported.
- The Discussion's headline — "we can explain about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) — summarizes no estimate shown: the two items enter only separately (Models 12 and 13). And the stronger of them is substantively a curriculum-support item in the same agree/disagree format, so its overlap with the outcome is close to built in; it does not measure concern about guilt as distinct from opposition to the content.
- The literature positioning is oversold in ways a citing reader should know. The 2024 project report the paper describes as having "only examined partisan views" (p.2) already reported the high-school majorities, an IRT scale, and the guilt hypothesis (literature reviewer's external check); the p.3 claim that "many" of the cited polls used opt-in panels fits only the Mood of the Nation poll, not Pew's probability panel or Monmouth's telephone samples; and Houston (2024, AERJ) on partisan sorting in education opinion, plus the political-science work on partisanship shaping racial attitudes, goes unmentioned. Two supporting citations on p.10 (Strauss 2023, whose title reports Moms for Liberty candidates losing; the "nationwide" book-challenge statistic) do not support the sentences they are attached to.
- Documentation stops short of what a reader needs to audit the inferential work. The p.3 sample arithmetic does not reconcile (2,005 + 1,900 equals the 3,905 responders, not the 4,896 invited; 3,905/4,896 is 79.8%, not 81%; six regression Ns exceed 3,905). The paper never states whether regressions or figures are weighted, what standard-error estimator is used (Table 3 has stars but no SEs), how the A/B forms were placed on one IRT scale, or which category is the county reference (the "County leans Democrat" row reads 0.00 in all eight columns although df_m implies four estimated county parameters). There is no data availability statement, replication code, software statement, or survey identifier, and the online appendix carrying Table A1 (all subgroup crosstabs), the elementary regressions, and the robustness checks does not travel with the PDF.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The UAS 567 methodology document reconciles the numbers, as the reproducibility sub-review anticipated: 4,896 households were invited, 3,974 responded to at least one item (81%), and 3,905 completed the survey (79.8%). The article pairs the completer count with the starter rate, and the regression Ns of 3,932–3,973 include partial respondents. The 81% is right, and the synthesis's "correction" of the contribution sub-review on this point was itself wrong. Whether the 2,005 and 1,900 "sampled" groups are responders rather than invitees is not affected. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the UAS 567 methodology documentation.

#### What to Rely On

- Grade-level topline support, always with the fielding date: among U.S. adults in fall 2023, all 18 race-related topics had majority support as appropriate for high school (56% to 92%) and 5 of 18 did for elementary school (Figure 1, p.6). The four most-supported topics are the same at both levels (equal treatment regardless of skin color, colonists harming Native Americans, interracial marriage rights, acting out civil-rights demonstrations).
- The size of the partisan divide on the scale: Democrats average 0.47 and Republicans −0.56 on the high-school theta, a gap of 1.03 (about 1.1 SD; p.7 and Table 3 Model 1), with Independents/neither at −0.61. The "about 30 percentage points" average item gap (p.7) is consistent with the party averages the text reports (87% vs 56% high school; 56% vs 26% elementary) but its item detail is in the unavailable Table A1.
- Place is mostly composition: county and state partisanship gaps are large bivariately (county strong Republican −0.51; state leans Republican −0.31; Models 3–4) and shrink to −0.09 or less once individual party identification is added (Model 8). This is the paper's best-supported analytic claim.
- Demographic gaps are smaller than partisan ones and are mostly absorbed by partisanship: the NH Black coefficient falls from 0.34 (Model 2) to 0.12 (Model 8), the parent coefficient from −0.28 (Model 7) to −0.16 (Model 8). Note that Model 8 adds all covariates at once, so "absorbed by partisanship" is approximate.
- Five of the six attitude items are strongly associated with the support scale (all p < .001 except LeadersWht at −0.04; Models 9–14), and the guilt and minority-authors items are the two most strongly associated with the partisan gap. The qualitative ordering is robust across baselines; the percentages are not.
- The instrument itself: Table 2 gives the full wording of every topic and attitude item, and the descriptive exhibits match the public UAS topline, so the item bank can be reused or compared against.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Concern about White guilt explains more than half of the partisan gap" (abstract, p.8, p.10) — the share is 42–49% against the like-for-like Model 8 baseline, is computed on an unexplained half-sample, and the item bundles support for teaching about historical racism with tolerance of guilt; it is a statistical-overlap share, not a mechanism.
- "About half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) — no joint model is reported; single-item shares are not additive when the items are correlated. Do not cite this as an estimate.
- Any "explains X%" percentage quoted from the prose — recompute it from Table 3 and state the baseline; the p.8 figures use Model 1 and the p.10 figures use Model 8.
- "Opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools" (abstract) — Figure 1 shows percent agree/strongly agree with "I'm not sure" in the denominator; 13 items below 50% support is not majority opposition, and the paper never reports the disagree share.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The UAS 567 topline, which reproduces Figure 1, reports the full response distribution: a majority disagree or strongly disagree on 10 of the 18 elementary-school topics, so the abstract's "opposition to most" is true, narrowly. The paper itself does not report the disagree shares, so the point that Figure 1 cannot show this stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the UAS 567 topline.

- "Majority support for 15 of 18 topics in deep-red states" (pp.7, 10; Figure 2) — "strong Republican" means 2020 Trump share of 65% or more, which by the reviewers' external reading of certified results is about four low-population states; no group N or confidence interval is reported, each item was seen by roughly half of those respondents, and several of the 15 majorities sit at 55–58%. Directionally informative, low precision.
- The opinion–policy incongruence and Fox News arguments in the Discussion (p.10) — the survey contains no measure of media exposure and the 18 items are never mapped onto what the state restrictions actually prohibit; the cited Fox News studies concern vote share and ideological polarization, not curriculum opinion, and press accounts of the one field experiment cited report racial attitudes largely unchanged.
- The novelty framing on p.3 — the "opt-in" criticism does not fit the Pew and Monmouth polls cited; the authors' own 2024 report already carried the high-school majorities and the guilt conjecture; cite Saavedra et al. (2024) for the partisan toplines and this article for the demographic/geographic breakdowns and the decomposition.
- The demographic "controls" — Table 3 contains no age, gender, religion, region, or urbanicity variables, so "net of demographics" means net of race, income, education, parent status, and county partisanship; the parent coefficient plausibly proxies age.
- The timing — fieldwork ended October 29, 2023; the Introduction is framed around the January 2025 executive order and a March 2026 count of 20 state bans, and the paper does not discuss whether opinion has moved since.
- Anything resting on the online appendix (Table A1 crosstabs and the 51- and 48-point item gaps, elementary regressions in A2, midpoint-coding robustness in A3–A4, item-level guilt models in A5–A6, the county version of Figure 2, and the theta distributions) — none of it was available to this review.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The descriptive core of the paper is sound: a probability-based panel with a high wave completion rate, weighting, and a thoughtful item bank that yields credible national estimates of support for 18 race-related topics and of large partisan gaps. The "what explains" analysis (RQ3) is much weaker than its framing suggests. The "percent of the partisan gap explained" figures are computed against shifting baselines and across samples of very different size. The key attitudinal "explanator" nearly restates the outcome. The Discussion's headline "about half ... based on two items" claim does not correspond to any estimated model. Readers should rely on the levels and gaps and treat the decomposition as loose, suggestive correlation.

**Strengths:**

- Probability-based, address-sampled panel (UAS) rather than an opt-in panel. There is a reported wave completion rate (p.3), survey-specific weights, and Rao-Scott-adjusted tests for the group comparisons (p.6). For national item-level percentages, this is about as good as online survey data get.
- The item bank is unusually granular: 18 concrete, behaviorally specific topics (Table 2, p.5), asked separately for elementary and high school, and pretested with two rounds of cognitive interviews (p.4). The wide spread in support across items (18% to 92%, Figure 1, p.6) lends credibility to the claim that respondents discriminated among items rather than answering by a single partisan reflex.
- Random assignment to parallel A/B forms, with within-form random item ordering (p.4), limits order effects. It also makes the forms statistically equivalent groups, which is what the IRT calibration needs to put the split item sets on a common scale.
- The IRT (graded response model) scaling is appropriate for ordinal items. The authors report a sensitivity check on treating "I'm not sure" as missing vs. midpoint, chosen by AIC/BIC (p.6; note 2, p.11), though the supporting tables are in the unavailable appendix.
- The authors explicitly disclaim causal interpretation of the attitudinal "explanations" (p.8) and acknowledge the descriptive nature of the findings (p.10).

**Weaknesses:**

- [Checkable] The "percent of the gap explained" claims use inconsistent or non-comparable baselines. Against Model 8, which has the same demographic controls as Models 9–14, the White-guilt item (Model 13) reduces the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.48 (49%) and the Neither coefficient from −0.52 to −0.30 (42%) (p.9, Table 3). The text's "more than half" (p.8) holds only against the bivariate Model 1 (53% and 51%), which has no controls and a different N. Similarly, "30% to 40%" for LrnAbtPOCgood (p.8) matches the Model 1 baseline (42%, 34%) better than Model 8 (36%, 23%). The "about 25%" figures for Models 10 and 14 (p.10) sit closer to the Model 8 baseline.
- [Checkable] Models 9–13 use roughly half the sample (N = 1,727–1,827) versus 3,892 in Model 8 and 3,818 in Model 14 (p.9, Table 3), and the text never explains why. Coefficient changes therefore mix "explanation" with sample change. Model 9, whose added item has a null coefficient (−0.04), already moves the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.88. That suggests a few percentage points of the "explained" share are pure sample composition.
- [Checkable] The Discussion states that "we can explain about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10). No model in Table 3 includes both LrnAbtWhtRacist and LrnAbtPOCgood (p.9; each enters alone in Models 13 and 12). Single-item shares are not additive when the items are correlated, so this sentence summarizes no estimate shown.
- [Interpretive] The strongest "explanatory" item nearly restates the outcome. "Children should learn about the ways White people have been racist historically ... even if that makes them feel guilty" (Table 2, p.5) is substantively a curriculum-support item, close to outcome topics like WhtBenSlav and WhtOppCivRights. It uses the same agree/disagree format in the same survey. Its absorbing the partisan coefficient is expected on measurement grounds alone and says little about mechanism. It also does not isolate "concern about White students feeling guilty" (abstract, p.1), because it bundles support for teaching about racism with tolerance of guilt.
- [Checkable] Regression Ns exceed the stated respondent count. The paper reports 3,905 responding households (p.3), yet Models 1–6 have N = 3,932 to 3,973 (p.9, Table 3). Either the unit counts differ (e.g., multiple respondents per household, which would call for household clustering that is never mentioned), or the counts are inconsistent. Also, the "sampled" groups of 2,005 and 1,900 (p.3) sum to exactly 3,905, the responder count, not the 4,896 invited. And 3,905/4,896 is 79.8%, not the stated 81% (p.3).

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The UAS 567 methodology document reconciles the numbers, as the reproducibility sub-review anticipated: 4,896 households were invited, 3,974 responded to at least one item (81%), and 3,905 completed the survey (79.8%). The article pairs the completer count with the starter rate, and the regression Ns of 3,932–3,973 include partial respondents. The 81% is right, and the synthesis's "correction" of the contribution sub-review on this point was itself wrong. Whether the 2,005 and 1,900 "sampled" groups are responders rather than invitees is not affected. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the UAS 567 methodology documentation.

- [Checkable] The text never says whether the regressions use survey weights or design-based standard errors (Methods, p.6). Table 3 reports only coefficients and stars, with no standard errors (p.9). In every column, df_r equals N − k − 1 (e.g., Model 1: 3,932 − 2 − 1 = 3,929), which is ordinary-regression residual df, not the design df a survey-design estimator would typically report.
- [Checkable] The county partisanship reference category is undefined and appears mis-displayed. "County leans Democrat" shows exactly 0.00, without stars, in all eight models that include county dummies. Yet df_m implies four estimated county parameters: Model 3 has df_m = 4, and Model 8's 17 = 2 party + 4 race + 4 county + 4 income + 2 education + 1 parent (p.9). The state dummies (Model 4) show "leans Democrat" as an estimated −0.04, so the state and county reference groups apparently differ. Apart from the state thresholds (≥65% and ≤35% Trump share, p.7), the county and state cutpoints are not defined.
- [Checkable] The demographic controls are thin. Table 3 contains no age, gender, religion, region, or urbanicity variables (p.9; the list is on p.5). "Net of demographics" therefore means net of race, income, education, parent status, and county partisanship only. Without age controls, the parent coefficient (−0.28 bivariate, −0.16 in Model 8) plausibly proxies age.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the national item-level levels (Figure 1, p.6) and the raw partisan gaps (about 30 points on average, p.7; theta gap 1.03, p.7 and Table 3 Model 1). These are well measured and consistent across the paper's exhibits.
- Read "item X explains Y% of the partisan gap" as roughly "adding item X shrinks the partisan coefficient by 20–50%, depending on the baseline and sample." Against the like-for-like Model 8 baseline, the guilt item accounts for roughly 42–49%, and the minority-authors item for roughly 23–36% (p.9, Table 3). These are statistical accounting shares, not mechanisms.
- Do not cite the "about half of the partisan gap based on two items" claim (p.10) as an estimate. No model supports it as stated.
- Treat the deep-red-state findings (Figure 2, p.8; "15 of 18" majority support, p.10) with caution. By external knowledge of 2020 results (not stated in the paper), a ≥65% Trump-share threshold captures only a handful of small states, and the paper reports no subgroup Ns or confidence intervals. Because of the A/B split, each item is answered by only about half of those respondents. Several of the 15 "majorities" are 55–61% and could plausibly fall within sampling error of 50%.
- The "Black-White gap reduced ~60% by partisanship" claim (p.8) compares Model 2 (0.34) with Model 8 (0.12), but Model 8 adds all demographics and county partisanship at once, not partisanship alone (p.9). Treat the attribution as approximate.
- The data are from September–October 2023 (p.3). Opinion may have moved after the 2025 federal actions described on p.1.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and question fit.* RQ1 and RQ2 are descriptive, and the design fits them well. RQ3 asks what "explains" partisan differences, and the title leads with that question. The only tool brought to it is sequential OLS with coefficient comparison: adding one attitude item at a time and reading off the shrinkage of the party coefficients. This is an informal mediation or decomposition exercise. Even setting causality aside, which the authors do (p.8), its results depend on sample, baseline, and ordering. A formal decomposition (e.g., Gelbach-style) with standard errors on the change, run on a common analytic sample, would be needed before the shares could be treated as quantities. The attitude items are also plausibly downstream of partisanship through cue-taking, or are co-indicators of the same latent construct as the outcome. In either case, "explained" means "statistically overlapping."

*Sample, weights, and counts.* Several reported counts do not reconcile, and none of the discrepancies is fatal, but together they limit how precisely readers can audit the work. The response rate arithmetic is 79.8%, not 81% (p.3). The subgroup sizes described as "sampled" equal the responders (p.3). Regression Ns of up to 3,973 exceed the 3,905 respondents (p.3; p.9, Table 3). Model 7 (parent only) has N = 3,905 exactly, while the other bivariate models are larger, which is also unexplained. The 81% figure is also a conditional wave completion rate among panel members. The cumulative response rate, which includes panel recruitment, is not reported and is presumably far lower. The weighting description (p.3) mentions panel selection and nonresponse but not the within-survey design: all K–12 households plus a random subsample of others. Whether the weights undo that oversampling cannot be verified from the text. Table 1 cannot settle it, because "Parent" (75.4% weighted vs. 69% national, p.4) is not defined as K–12 parent versus ever-parent. Table 1 also shows non-trivial income deviations: 21.3% vs. 15.2% under \$25,000, and 14.1% vs. 21.5% over \$150,000 (p.4). "Quite similar" (p.3) is somewhat generous, although the comparison mixes person-level sample shares with household-level census income.

*See the correction note in the Methods sub-review above: the 81% is the starter rate.*

*Measurement.* The A/B split means each respondent's theta rests on at most nine items per grade band, and fewer after "I'm not sure" responses are set to missing (p.4, p.6). Scale reliability and unidimensionality diagnostics are not reported in the text, and the appendix was not available to check them. Using predicted thetas, likely EAP-type, as dependent variables attenuates group differences toward zero when the scoring model does not condition on covariates. The partisan coefficients are therefore probably conservative in absolute terms, though this matters less for the relative-shrinkage comparisons. The attitude items appear to enter as single linear terms (each adds one df, p.9), and their scaling is not stated, so coefficient magnitudes such as 0.49 or 0.45 cannot be read in natural units. For the item-level percentages, the Figure 1 note (p.6) defines support as agree or strongly agree but does not say whether "I'm not sure" responses remain in the denominator. That matters for the abstract's claim of "opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools" (p.1). Figure 1 shows only agreement shares, so "below 50% agree" is not the same as majority opposition if not-sure responses are counted. The text says Figure 1 shows "support and opposition" (p.6), but it shows support only.

*See the correction note under What to Treat Cautiously: the UAS topline shows majority disagreement on 10 of 18.*

*Internal consistency that checks out.* Several text-to-exhibit claims do verify. There are five elementary items above 50% and eight below one-third (Figure 1, p.6; two sit at 33%). Four of the top five items are the same across grade bands. The high school range is 56% at minimum (Figure 1). There are 15 of 18 majorities in strong-Republican states (Figure 2, p.8). The Democrat–Republican theta gap of 1.03 matches the Model 1 coefficient, and the Model 1 constant of 0.47 matches the reported Democratic mean (p.7; p.9). The parent gap is "cut approximately in half" (−0.28 to −0.16), and the county strong-Republican gap is "almost completely explained" (−0.51 to −0.09) (p.9, Models 3, 7, 8). "Five of six items strongly predict" is consistent with the null LeadersWht coefficient (p.9, Model 9). One minor inconsistency: note 3 (p.11) says state partisanship was omitted from Models 9–14, but Table 3 shows it is also absent from Model 8 (p.9).

*Bottom line.* The paper's descriptive contribution, what the public supports item by item and by grade band and how large the partisan divide is, is load-bearing and credible. The geographic comparisons are directionally informative but under-documented. The attitudinal "explanation" of partisan gaps is the paper's most-cited analytic move and its most fragile. The quantitative shares shift by 5–15 percentage points depending on baseline. The analytic sample halves without explanation. The central item overlaps conceptually with the outcome. The two-item "about half" claim is unestimated. None of this reverses the qualitative point that attitudes about racism-and-guilt and about diverse perspectives are strongly correlated with the partisan divide. But the precise percentages should not be carried forward.

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper sets out the policy context briskly and reports the prior polls it cites accurately. But its four-part gap statement (p.3) oversells what is new. It understates how much of this survey's evidence already appeared in the authors' own 2024 project report. It misdescribes how the prior polls it cites were sampled. And it does not engage the political-science literature on racial attitudes and partisan sorting, which bears directly on its central "what explains partisan gaps" question. The Discussion's use of Fox News research (p.10) goes beyond what that research shows. The paper's real contributions are an 18-item topic battery, subgroup and county/state breakdowns from a probability panel, and a regression decomposition of the partisan gap. Those contributions are narrower than the framing suggests.

**Strengths:**

- The prior polls it cites are quoted accurately. I checked two. The Monmouth figures (94% of Democrats vs. 54% of Republicans on the "history of racism"; 75% vs. 16% on CRT; p.3) match press reports of that poll. The Helmstetter and Plutzer framing (near-consensus on teaching historical slavery, roughly half support for teaching its ongoing effects) matches the APM/McCourtney release.
- It correctly identifies the most important finding from earlier polling: support splits by party when the topic moves from historical slavery to present-day inequality (pp.2–3). It then tests that pattern with a much larger set of specific items (Table 2, p.5).
- The Background (p.2) links the argument to evidence on curriculum effects, including Dee and Penner (2017), Bonilla et al. (2021), and Hughes et al. (2007). This reminds readers that the contested content has measured effects on students and is not only a symbolic fight.
- Citing Lax and Phillips (2009, 2012) on opinion–policy incongruence (p.10) is the right way to frame the finding that majorities in deep-red states support most high-school items (Figure 2, p.8).

**Weaknesses:**

- **Overlap with the authors' own report is understated (checkable).** On p.2 the paper says the project report (Saavedra et al., 2024) "only examined partisan views." I obtained the report from the URL in the reference list (p.13). It uses the same September 19–October 29, 2023 UAS survey and the same 18 race items. It already reports majority support for all 18 items in high school, which is the paper's RQ1 headline. It already reports an IRT scale of support and names "embracing differences" as the strongest purpose-of-education predictor (r = 0.33). And it already reports the 81% vs. 33% partisan split on the White-guilt item, suggesting guilt "could be a driving factor in the pushback." What is genuinely new here is the non-partisan demographic and geographic breakdowns and the regression decomposition behind RQ3 (Table 3, p.9).
- **The opt-in claim in the gap statement is inaccurate for the studies cited (checkable).** On p.3 the paper says "many of the aforementioned survey studies are based on opt-in online panels." Of the three prior surveys it names, only the Mood of the Nation poll (Helmstetter & Plutzer, 2022) uses an opt-in panel: YouGov with matching, according to the McCourtney Institute's methods page. Pew surveys like the 2022 one cited come from Pew's probability-based American Trends Panel. Monmouth's 2021 national polls were telephone probability samples, to my knowledge. So probability sampling is not a clean point of novelty.
- **"No studies… attempt to understand the factors" (p.3) is too strong.** Within education research, Houston (2024, *American Educational Research Journal*, "Polarization, Partisan Sorting, and the Politics of Education") decomposes widening partisan gaps in education opinion, including race-related items from the Education Next survey, into sorting and polarization. It finds that people mostly change issue positions to match their party. The paper cites none of this work.
- **No engagement with political science on racial attitudes.** The explanatory items in Table 2 (e.g., LrnAbtWhtRacist, LeadersWht, WhtBksImport) are close relatives of racial-attitude measures. The paper's finding that they "explain" about half the partisan gap (p.10) echoes a large literature on racial resentment and the racialization of party identity (Kinder & Sanders, 1996; Tesler, 2016). It also runs into Engelhardt (2021, *British Journal of Political Science*), which uses panel data to show that partisanship shapes White Americans' racial attitudes. That result complicates reading these items as the drivers of partisan differences.
- **The Fox News evidence is used beyond what it shows (partly checkable).** The Introduction (p.1) and Discussion (p.10) cite Fox News studies of vote share and ideological polarization to suggest that Fox rhetoric shaped Republicans' views on race curriculum. None of the cited studies measures curriculum opinion. Press coverage of Broockman and Kalla's field experiment, the only causal study cited on attitudes, reports that attitudes about race, policing, and climate were largely unchanged. The same p.10 sentence also calls this "high-quality evidence" while grouping an observational PLOS One study (Earle & Hodson, 2022) with causal designs.
- **Some supporting citations do not support the specific claims (checkable).** "11 people responsible for more than half of the book ban requests nationwide" (p.10) comes from a Washington Post records analysis of about 100 responding districts, not a national count. The Strauss (2023) article, cited for "the election of school board candidates who aim to restrict curriculum" (p.10), reports that Moms for Liberty candidates lost in November 2023. Cabrera et al. (2014), cited for 1990s attacks on multicultural curricula (p.2), is about the 2010s Tucson Mexican American Studies controversy.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- For topline and partisan item-level results, and for the first statement of the guilt hypothesis, cite Saavedra et al. (2024). Cite this paper for the demographic and county/state breakdowns and for the regression decomposition of the partisan gap.
- Read Houston (2024, *AERJ*) alongside this paper. It is the closest antecedent on why education opinion splits by party, and its sorting result gives a different mechanism from "attitudes explain partisanship." Houston and Barone (2024, EdWorkingPaper 24-919), a synthesis of 18 elite-cue experiments on education policy, is a better guide than the Fox News vote-share papers to how partisan elites move education opinion.
- Treat the "half the gap is explained" result (p.10) as a finding about attitudes that move together with party, not about causes. Engelhardt (2021) and Tesler (2016) explain why the causal arrow may run from party to racial attitudes.
- Check the "opt-in," "nationwide," and Strauss citations on p.3 and p.10 before repeating them.
- For more probability-panel evidence on similar topics, see Gallup's 2023 poll "Majorities Support Racial Education in U.S. Schools." It used a sample that combined the probability-based Gallup Panel with an opt-in supplement and reported breakdowns by party and by race. On school board and interest-group mobilization, which the paper's "asymmetric mobilization" argument leans on, see Anzia (2014, *Timing and Turnout*) and Berkman and Plutzer (2005, *Ten Thousand Democracies*).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Novelty claims.* The four-part gap statement on p.3 is the paper's main positioning claim.

- Part one: prior work "tends to only focus on one or a few broad topics." This is fair. An 18-item battery of concrete classroom scenarios (Table 2) is more granular than any earlier poll I know of. Gallup (2023) asked about four topics.
- Part two: prior work focuses "exclusively on partisan splits." This is overstated. Gallup (2023) reported results by race as well, and Pew reports routinely include race breakdowns. County- and state-level context (Figure 2; Table 3 Models 4–5) is genuinely less common.
- Part three: the opt-in claim. This is inaccurate for the studies cited, as described above.
- Part four: "no studies… attempt to understand the factors." This holds only if "factors" is limited to curriculum opinion measured with scenario items. Even then, Houston (2024) is a close antecedent that the paper does not engage.

Readers should take the defensible novelty to be granularity plus a decomposition exercise, not the first explanation of these gaps.

*The authors' own pipeline.* The reference list contains three outputs from the same project. All appear to rest on the 2022 and 2023 UAS waves: Polikoff et al. (2022), Saavedra et al. (2024), and the sibling LGBTQ paper, Polikoff et al. (2025). The paper is clear that the LGBTQ paper is "similar work" (p.2). It is less clear about the 2024 report. Having checked that report, I would describe this article as a peer-reviewed extension of it. RQ1, most of the partisan half of RQ2, the IRT scale, and the guilt interpretation were all public before submission. That matters for citation and credit, and it matters for reading the Discussion. The claim that "it is not especially surprising that this item explained the largest portion of the partisan gap" (p.10) confirms the authors' own earlier conjecture. It is not an independent discovery.

*Adjacent fields.* The most consequential omission is political science on race and partisanship. The paper frames partisanship as a social identity (Abramowitz & Saunders, 2006; Mason & Wronski, 2018; p.2). But it does not follow that framing to its obvious implication, which is that partisans adopt the positions their side takes. Elite-cue and sorting research makes this point, both in general (e.g., Lenz, 2012, *Follow the Leader?*) and in education specifically (Houston, 2024; Houston & Barone, 2024). The Houston and Barone synthesis finds that endorsements by high-profile partisans mostly polarize education opinion rather than shift it overall. That fits the pattern here better than a persuasion story tied to Fox News. Relatedly, social psychology has studied White guilt and its link to racial-policy attitudes (e.g., Swim & Miller, 1999; Iyer, Leach & Crosby, 2003). That work would help readers interpret the paper's single most important explanatory item, LrnAbtWhtRacist. The paper does not engage it.

*Conflicting evidence and the paper's own citations.* The Discussion suggests telling the public that "students do not routinely feel guilt from these lessons (if that is true)" (p.11). But one of the paper's own background citations, Hughes, Bigler and Levy (2007), bears directly on this question. As summarized in public descriptions of that study, White children who received lessons about historical racism held less biased attitudes and valued racial fairness more. They also showed more defensiveness, and those older than about seven reported more racial guilt. So the fuller evidence suggests that some guilt does occur, alongside attitude benefits. That supports the paper's alternative suggestion ("some guilt… can be valuable or productive") more than the first one. The Monmouth split-sample result the paper cites (p.3) is also more instructive than the paper lets on. Wording the topic as "history of racism" versus "critical race theory" moves support dramatically, which is a reminder that the paper's item wordings (e.g., "benefited," "hurtful") are part of what is being measured. The framing literature (e.g., Chong & Druckman, 2007) is relevant but not cited.

*CRT and "divisive concepts" legislation.* The policy context relies mostly on journalism: Education Week's map, Washington Post pieces, and Fox transcripts (pp.1–2, p.10). There is now a scholarly and grey literature it could draw on. It includes RAND's teacher surveys on instructional limits (Woo et al., 2023, "Walking on Eggshells"), UCLA IDEA's studies of the "conflict campaign" and its chilling effects (Pollock et al., 2022; Rogers & Kahne, 2022), and PEN America's tracking of "educational gag orders." The historical account of 1990s fights would be better supported by Nash, Crabtree and Dunn (1997, *History on Trial*) than by Cabrera et al. (2014). None of this changes the paper's descriptive findings. It does mean readers get a thinner picture of the field than the topic warrants.

*What I checked and what I could not.* I used web search to check the following: the Mood of the Nation poll's methods; the Monmouth figures; the Gallup 2023 poll; Houston (2024) and Houston and Barone (2024); Engelhardt (2021); Mercer and Lau (2023), a Pew benchmarking study finding opt-in samples roughly half as accurate as probability panels; the Washington Post book-challenge analysis; and press summaries of Broockman and Kalla. I downloaded and searched the text of Saavedra et al. (2024). I did not read the full texts of Hughes et al. (2007) or Broockman and Kalla, and characterizations of those rely on abstracts and press summaries. I could not verify whether Mercer and Lau (2023) support the claim that probability panels have "lower levels of social desirability bias" (p.3). The report is about benchmark accuracy, and readers should check that attribution. The online appendix (Tables A1–A6, Figures A1–A2) was not available to me and plays no role in this assessment. Other literature on public opinion about curriculum may exist that I am not aware of.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is short, plainly written, and easy to navigate. Its descriptive core (Figure 1, Figure 2, and the Results narrative on pp.6–7) is reported accurately: every count I checked against the bar charts matches. The regression section, which the title and abstract put front and center ("What Explains..."), is where the prose outruns Table 3. The "share of the partisan gap explained" figures switch baselines from claim to claim and compare coefficients across samples of very different size. The Discussion's "two items explain about half" rests on no model shown. Table 3 has presentation errors that leave the reader unable to tell some reference categories, and the sample counts on p.3 do not reconcile with the regression Ns.

**Strengths:**

- The descriptive narrative on pp.6–7 tracks Figure 1 (p.6) closely. The five elementary items above 50%, the eight below one-third, majority high-school support for all 18 items, and "four of the top five" all check out exactly against the bar values.
- The paper is easy to navigate. The three research questions (p.2) map one-to-one onto the three Results subsections (pp.6–8), and the Methods (p.6) are organized the same way, so a reader can go straight to the answer to any question.
- Table 2 (p.5) gives the full wording for every topic and attitude item. That lets a reader see exactly what "support" means for each topic, which matters a great deal for items whose short labels ("gun violence," "White guilt") carry interpretive weight.
- The bar charts are honestly drawn. Both use a 0–100% axis with printed values on every bar, and the Figure 2 note defines support. The "15 of 18" deep-red-state claim (pp.7, 10) is directly verifiable from Figure 2 (p.8).
- The authors say more than once that the regressions are descriptive and not causal (pp.8, 10). That caveat is well placed right next to the headline "White guilt" result.

**Weaknesses:**

- The percent-of-gap-explained claims (pp.8, 10) cannot all be reproduced against a single baseline. "More than half" for LrnAbtWhtRacist holds only against bivariate Model 1 (53%/51%). Against Model 8 it is 49%/42%. Meanwhile, "about 25%" for LrnAbtPOCbad and TchImpEmbraceDiff holds only against Model 8, and it is roughly 30–36% against Model 1.
- Models 9–13 (p.9) are estimated on 1,727–1,827 respondents, versus 3,892 in Model 8, and the text never explains the drop. So the "explained" shares mix attenuation with changes in sample composition. Model 9, whose attitude item is null (−0.04), already moves the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.88 and the Neither coefficient from −0.52 to −0.55.
- The Discussion (p.10) says "about half of the partisan gaps" is explained "based on two items." No model in Table 3 includes both items: Models 12 and 13 each enter one. The sentence reads as a joint result that the paper never shows.
- The sample bookkeeping does not reconcile. The two sampled groups on p.3 (2,005 + 1,900) sum to the 3,905 respondents, not the 4,896 invited. 3,905/4,896 is 79.8%, not 81%. And six of the Table 3 models report Ns (3,932–3,973) larger than 3,905.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The UAS 567 methodology document reconciles the numbers, as the reproducibility sub-review anticipated: 4,896 households were invited, 3,974 responded to at least one item (81%), and 3,905 completed the survey (79.8%). The article pairs the completer count with the starter rate, and the regression Ns of 3,932–3,973 include partial respondents. The 81% is right, and the synthesis's "correction" of the contribution sub-review on this point was itself wrong. Whether the 2,005 and 1,900 "sampled" groups are responders rather than invitees is not affected. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the UAS 567 methodology documentation.

- Table 3 (p.9) is hard to read on its own. There are no standard errors. The note does not name the reference category for any variable set, and it defines "HS = Hispanic" although the row says "Hispanic" and Table 1 uses HS for high school. The "County leans Democrat" row shows 0.00 in all eight columns, even though df_m implies four estimated county parameters.
- The abstract says respondents show "opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools." Figure 1 measures only percent agree/strongly agree, on a scale that included "I'm not sure," and it does not state the denominator. Below-50% support is shown, but majority opposition is not.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Figure 1 (p.6) and Figure 2 (p.8) directly. They are the paper's most reliable evidence, and the prose summarizing them can be trusted.
- Before quoting any "explains X% of the partisan gap" figure, work it out yourself from Table 3 (p.9) and say which baseline you used. The Model 1 and Model 8 baselines give noticeably different answers (see the checks below). Also keep in mind that Models 9–13 use roughly half the sample.
- Do not cite the Discussion's "two items explain about half" (p.10) as a joint estimate. The paper reports only one-item-at-a-time models.
- Treat "opposition" in the abstract as "less than majority agreement." Treat the "White guilt" label as shorthand for a compound item that asks whether children should learn about historical White racism "even if that makes them feel guilty" (Table 2, p.5). It does not directly measure concern about guilt.
- You can skim the Background (pp.2–3) and the Fox News paragraphs (pp.1, 10). The data contain no measure of media exposure, so those passages are context and speculation, not findings.
- Much of the RQ2 narrative (p.7: party-by-item majorities, the 51- and 48-point gaps, education and race gaps), all elementary-level regressions, and the county version of Figure 2 live in the online appendix (Tables A1–A6, Figures A1–A2). The appendix was not available for this review, so those claims are unverified here.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization.* The paper follows a conventional structure, and the Results subsections are titled with the research questions. The load-bearing exhibits are Figure 1 (RQ1), Figure 2 (the geography claim that drives the policy argument in the Discussion), and Table 3 (RQ3). Figure 1 and Figure 2 are self-contained apart from missing Ns. Figure 1's labels are a third naming scheme: Table 2's abbreviations never appear in either figure, despite the p.4 statement that the short names are used "throughout the text and tables." Table 3 is the densest exhibit and the least self-contained. It gives no standard errors, no reference categories, and no indication of which models use the reduced sample. It does not say how the attitude items are coded, so the coefficients of 0.45 or 0.49 cannot be read as effect sizes. The row definitions for the county and state categories are also incomplete: only the "strong" cutoffs are given, on p.7.

*Fidelity of the RQ3 narrative.* The Model 1 vs. Model 8 comparison on p.8 is described fairly in direction. "Essentially unchanged" is a little generous: the Republican gap shrinks 9% and the Neither gap 15%, and the sample changes from 3,932 to 3,892. The demographic-attenuation claims (Black-White about 60%, parent about half) roughly match the arithmetic from Model 2/7 to Model 8 (65% and 43%). But the text credits the reduction to "the addition of partisan identifiers," whereas Model 8 adds all demographics and county partisanship simultaneously. No model isolates partisanship. The attitude section has the larger problem. The headline "more than half" is true only against Model 1, which has no controls and uses a different sample. The "about 25%" claims are true only against Model 8. Because Models 9–13 draw on subsamples of roughly 1,730–1,830, even the coefficient-to-coefficient comparison is not like-for-like. The claim that demographic coefficients are "mostly unchanged" between Model 8 and Models 12–13 is also loose. In Model 13 the NH Black coefficient goes from 0.12* to −0.03, and the parent coefficient falls by about a third. Interpretively, calling the guilt item a measure of "beliefs that these topics are associated with White students' guilt" (p.8) goes beyond the item's wording, and the abstract's "concern about White students feeling guilty" goes further still. The item is close in content to the outcome battery itself, which a reader should keep in mind when reading "explains."

*Abstract.* The abstract accurately conveys the sample type and the elementary/high-school contrast. It overstates "opposition." It describes attitude items as "strongly predictive of partisan gaps" when the analysis is about attenuation. "Valuing diverse contributions" is ambiguous: it could mean LrnAbtPOCgood or TchImpEmbraceDiff. The abstract also omits that the data are from fall 2023, that the analysis is descriptive, and the deep-red-state result that anchors the Discussion.

**Text-vs-exhibit checks**

Sample and descriptives

1. p.3: sampled groups n = 2,005 + 1,900 = 3,905 vs. "4,896 households invited, 3,905 responded" (p.3). **MISMATCH** (internal): the group sizes equal the respondent count, not the invited count.
2. p.3: "response rate of 81%" vs. 3,905/4,896 = 79.8%. **MISMATCH** (minor).

   *See the correction note in the Writing sub-review above: the 81% is the starter rate.*

3. p.3: 3,905 respondents vs. Table 3 (p.9) N = 3,932 (M1), 3,973 (M2, M4, M6), 3,969 (M3), 3,967 (M5). **MISMATCH**; no explanation given. Only M7 equals 3,905.
4. p.3: weighted sample "quite similar" to targets vs. Table 1 (p.4): income <\$25k 21.3 vs. 15.2; >\$150k 14.1 vs. 21.5; parent 75.4 vs. 69; NH White 61.3 vs. 57.1. **Partial MISMATCH** (interpretive): differences of 6–7 points on income and parental status, and these are weighted figures. Table 1 has no N and no partisanship row. All column totals sum to 100 (MATCH).
5. p.4: 18 topics, five reason items and one purpose item vs. Table 2 (p.5). **MATCH**.
6. p.4: shortened names used "throughout the text and tables" vs. Figures 1–2 (pp.6, 8), which use plain-language labels, and prose that quotes full items. **MISMATCH**.
7. p.6 Methods: "we report mean responses to each of the 18 topics" vs. Figure 1, which shows percent agree/strongly agree. **MISMATCH**.
8. p.6: "Figure 1 shows the support and opposition" vs. Figure 1, which shows support only. **MISMATCH**.

31. "Five of the six items strongly predict" theta: LeadersWht −0.04 is not significant; the other five are all p < .001. **MATCH**.
32. LrnAbtWhtRacist "explains more than half" of both gaps (M13: Republican −0.48, Neither −0.30). Against Model 1: 53% / 51%, **MATCH (barely)**. Against Model 8: 49% / 42%, **MISMATCH**. N is 1,727.
33. LrnAbtPOCgood "approximately 30% to 40%" (M12: −0.60, −0.40). Against M1: 42% / 34%. Against M8: 36% / 23%. **Partial MATCH**; the Neither gap against Model 8 falls short.
34. LrnAbtPOCbad and TchImpEmbraceDiff "about 25%" each (M10: −0.72/−0.39; M14: −0.74/−0.42). Against M8: 23%/25% and 21%/19%, **MATCH**. Against M1: 30%/36% and 28%/31%, **MISMATCH**. Items 32–34 are therefore not mutually consistent on any single baseline.
35. The drop in N from Model 8 (3,892) to Models 9–13 (1,746; 1,827; 1,784; 1,732; 1,727), with Model 14 back at 3,818. **CANNOT CHECK**: the text is silent. Presumably the reason items went to a subsample, but the paper does not say so.
36. Demographic coefficients "mostly unchanged" between M8 and M12/M13 (p.8): NH Black 0.12* to 0.12* / −0.03; NH Asian −0.10 to −0.12 / −0.20**; parent −0.16*** to −0.11** / −0.10*; county strong Republican −0.09* to −0.06 / −0.08 (both not significant). **Partial MISMATCH**.
37. Discussion "about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10). **CANNOT CHECK / unsupported**: no Table 3 model includes both items.
38. Table 3 note "HS = Hispanic" vs. the row label "Hispanic," and Table 1's "HS = high school." **MISMATCH**. "NH" is not defined in the Table 3 note.
39. "County leans Democrat" = 0.00 in Models 3 and 8–14, with no reference category stated. Model 3 df_m = 4 (and 3,969 − 4 − 1 = 3,964 = df_r) implies four estimated county parameters, but only three nonzero rows are shown. **Internal inconsistency; CANNOT RESOLVE**. By analogy with Model 4 (four state rows, df_m = 4), the omitted category is presumably "strong Democrat," which makes an exact 0.00 across eight models implausible as an estimate.
40. df_r = N − df_m − 1 in all 14 columns. **MATCH**.
41. Income top-category labels: "Greater than \$150,000" (Table 1), "\$150,000 or more" (p.5), "More than \$150,000" (Table 3). **Minor inconsistency**. There is also a typo, "sqaures," on p.6.
42. The p.7 statement that theta reflects "the 18 race-related items" vs. p.4, where each respondent was randomized to one form covering 9 of the 18. **Minor inconsistency** worth knowing when reading theta.

*Density.* At 13 pages the paper is lean. Readers should not skip Table 3 or its N row. They can skim the Background and the media-effects framing.

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's lasting contribution is descriptive. It gives item-level public opinion on 18 specific race-related curriculum topics, asked separately for elementary and high school grades, from a probability-based national panel, broken down by partisanship, demographics, and state and county political context. That is a useful benchmark on a question where most earlier evidence came from one or two broad items or from opt-in panels. The explanatory contribution promised by the title is much thinner. Regressing one race-curriculum attitude on another, closely related one, measured in the same cross-section, shows correlation, not explanation. The best-known numbers (a two-item "about half" of the partisan gap, majority support in "deep-red states") are less secure than the way the paper presents them.

**Strengths:**

- **Finer-grained measurement than earlier polls.** Checkable: 18 topics, each rated separately for Grades K–5 and 9–12, span easy items (equal treatment regardless of skin color, 92% high school support) to hard ones (math project on office referrals by race, 56%) (p.4, Table 2; p.6, Figure 1). Earlier surveys the paper cites mostly asked about slavery, present-day effects, or "CRT" (p.3). The grade-level contrast is the paper's most useful new finding: 5 of 18 items have majority support in elementary grades, against 18 of 18 in high school (pp.6–7, Figure 1).
- **Better sample than most comparators.** Checkable: the UAS uses address-based probability sampling, and 3,905 of 4,896 invited households responded (81%), with weighting for selection and nonresponse (p.3). The earlier CRT and slavery polls, by the paper's own account, often used opt-in panels (p.3). This makes the toplines more credible than most of the prior numbers.
- **Geography versus individual partisanship.** Checkable: bivariate county and state gaps (for example, county strong Republican −0.51, state leans Republican −0.31; p.9, Table 3, Models 3–4) mostly disappear once individual party ID is added (county strong Republican −0.09, Model 8). Partisan coefficients barely change when demographics are added (Republican −1.03 in Model 1 vs. −0.94 in Model 8). This is a clean, citable descriptive decomposition: place-based differences in opinion are mostly differences in who lives there.
- **Hedges are present.** Checkable: the paper says the attitude results "should not be seen as a causal explanation" (p.8), calls its findings "descriptive" (p.10), and says it does "not claim causal evidence" on Fox News (p.10).

**Weaknesses:**

- **"Explains about half" is looser than Table 3 supports.** Checkable: the Discussion says two items together "explain about half" of the partisan gap (p.10). The two items are only ever entered separately (Models 12 and 13); no model includes both (p.9, Table 3). Against the comparable baseline with demographic controls (Model 8), the White-racism/guilt item cuts the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.48 (49%) and the Neither coefficient from −0.52 to −0.30 (42%). The text says "more than half" (p.8), which holds only against the bivariate Model 1 (53% and 51%).
- **The attitude models use a different, roughly half-size sample.** Checkable: Models 9–13 have N = 1,727–1,827, against 3,892 in Model 8 (p.9, Table 3). The paper does not explain why, and it reports no Model 8 baseline on the same subsample. So the "share explained" mixes the effect of adding the attitude with the change of sample. A related oddity: Models 1–6 report N up to 3,973, more than the 3,905 respondents reported on p.3 (p.9, Table 3). The paper does not explain this either.
- **The "guilt" item does not isolate guilt.** Checkable: the item reads "Children should learn about the ways White people have been racist historically in the U.S. even if that makes them feel guilty" (p.5, Table 2). The Abstract calls it "concern about White students feeling guilty" (p.1). Judgment: someone can disagree because they object to the content, not the guilt. The item then works almost as another outcome item, and its strong link to the outcome scale (R² rises to .45, Model 13) is close to built in. The paper cannot separate "guilt concern" from "opposition to teaching about White racism."
- **Policy and media claims go beyond the data.** Judgment: the opinion–policy incongruence argument (p.10) never maps the 18 items onto what the actual restrictions prohibit, so "majority support" for a topic being "appropriate" is not shown to conflict with any specific law. The Fox News and asymmetric-mobilization paragraph (p.10) draws on no measure in this survey.
- **The data are dated relative to the framing, and the paper doesn't say so.** Checkable: fieldwork ran September 19 to October 29, 2023 (p.3). The Introduction frames the paper around the January 2025 executive order and a March 2026 count of 20 states with restrictions (pp.1–2). The paper does not discuss whether opinion moved in the roughly two and a half years between fieldwork and publication.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for grade-level topline support.** Among U.S. adults in fall 2023, every one of 18 race-related topics had majority support as appropriate for high school (56–92%), but only 5 did for elementary school (p.6, Figure 1). Always attach the fielding date.
- **Cite it for place effects being mostly partisanship.** Individual partisanship, not state or county context, accounts for most place-based differences in support (p.9, Table 3, Models 3–4 vs. 8). This is its best-supported analytic claim.
- **Cite the partisan gap with care.** Support on the IRT scale differs by party by about 1 SD (p.7). The "about 30 percentage points" average item gap (p.7) rests on appendix Table A1, which was not available to this reviewer. The party-level averages in the text (87% vs. 56% at high school, 56% vs. 26% at elementary; p.7) agree with it.
- **Do not cite it for "concern about White guilt explains half the partisan divide."** Single items entered separately account for roughly 40–50% (guilt item) and 23–36% (diverse-books item) of the adjusted partisan coefficients, in a subsample, with no joint model. The guilt item mixes content opposition with guilt.
- **Do not cite it for "majority support in deep-red states" without its definition.** "Strong Republican" means states with 2020 Trump share of at least 65% (p.7). The paper does not list these states or give their sample size. By my reading of certified 2020 returns, only about four low-population states meet that bar. Three of the 18 items fall below 50% there, and several of the rest are at 55–58% (p.8, Figure 2).
- **Do not cite it for "curriculum bans contradict public opinion" or for Fox News effects.** Neither was tested (p.10).
- **Open questions:** whether the attitudes precede or follow partisan cues (this needs panel data or experiments); whether opinion has shifted since 2023; how "not sure" responses, which count against "support" (p.6, Figure 1 note), change the elementary "opposition" reading; and whether support holds for the specific statutory language of existing bans.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is new.* The paper states its advance over the authors' 2024 project report plainly: that report "only examined partisan views on these topics" (p.2), and the authors' 2022 report covered "just a few race-related topics" (p.2). The additions here are demographic and geographic breakdowns, an IRT scale, and regressions on attitude items. Judgment: the item-level partisan toplines were largely public already, so the article's added value lies mainly in the geography decomposition and the attitude regressions. The first of these is solid. The second is the weaker part. I did not check the 2024 report's contents directly. The survey also produced a companion paper on LGBTQ topics (Polikoff et al., 2025, cited p.2), so this article is one of several outputs from a single wave.

*The three quotable claims, ranked by support.* (i) Majority high-school support for all 18 topics is directly visible in Figure 1 (p.6) and is the strongest claim, though "support" means agree or strongly agree out of all responses including "not sure." That makes the high-school majorities conservative, and it makes the Abstract's "opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools" (p.1) overstated: 13 items below 50% support is not the same as majority opposition. The deep-red-state extension (15 of 18; pp.7, 10; Figure 2) is weaker. It rests on a small, undisclosed group of states with no reported sample size or confidence intervals, and the Discussion's pairing of this finding with the states that "most aggressively pursued" restrictions (p.10) assumes an overlap the paper does not show. (ii) The roughly 30-point partisan gap is internally consistent with the party averages on p.7, but its item detail sits in an appendix I could not see. (iii) The "about half" claim is the least secure, for the reasons given above: separate models, a changed sample, a baseline that differs between p.8 and the arithmetic, and a key regressor that nearly overlaps the outcome.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The UAS 567 topline, which reproduces Figure 1, reports the full response distribution: a majority disagree or strongly disagree on 10 of the 18 elementary-school topics, so the abstract's "opposition to most" is true, narrowly. The paper itself does not report the disagree shares, so the point that Figure 1 cannot show this stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the UAS 567 topline.

*Does the paper answer its title?* Only in the weak sense of variance decomposition. In a single cross-section, the mediation reading (attitude drives support, partisanship drives the attitude) cannot be told apart from the reverse, or from party identity driving both. Party identity was measured at the end of the same survey (p.5). The hedges on p.8 and p.10 are real, but they are outweighed by the title, by an Abstract that names the two attitudes as "strongly predictive of partisan gaps" (p.1), and by Discussion recommendations such as designing "less guilt-inducing" lessons (p.11). That last recommendation is appropriately conditional ("if concerns... are indeed animating conservative opposition"). The Fox News passage is less restrained ("hardly a stretch," p.10). Judgment: the hedging is proportionate in the Results and falls short in the title, Abstract, and policy paragraphs.

*Generalizability.* The national probability design supports U.S.-adult inferences as of late 2023. Checkable: the weighted sample over-represents households under \$25,000 (21.3% vs. 15.2%) and under-represents those over \$150,000 (14.1% vs. 21.5%) (p.4, Table 1). Income is positively related to support (p.9, Table 3, Model 5), so this matters at the margin, though the direction of any bias is not obvious once partisanship is taken into account. Findings are specific to item wording. Several items were deliberately made concrete (for example, the sexual-assault detail added after cognitive interviews, p.4), and the paper is clear that support varies sharply with framing. Elementary-level regressions are in appendix Table A2, which I could not see. With one cross-section, trend claims are not possible.

*Standing.* Judgment: for item-level, grade-specific U.S. opinion on race-related curriculum topics, this is now probably the best single published probability-sample benchmark. It should replace the one-item slavery and CRT polls as the default citation for "what topics do Americans accept at which grade." It is not the best evidence on *why* partisans differ, and it does not show that curriculum restrictions are out of step with public opinion. Both are hypotheses it sets up for panel, experimental, or policy-text-matched follow-up work.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The underlying microdata are, as far as I can tell, publicly downloadable. The paper's descriptive exhibits (Table 1, Figure 1) match the public UAS topline to the percentage point. But the article itself does not document enough to rebuild the regression analysis behind its headline claim (RQ3, Table 3). It has no data availability statement, no code, no software statement and no survey identifier. It never says whether the regressions are weighted or how standard errors are computed. The IRT scoring is underspecified, and the sample description on p. 3 conflicts with the survey's own documentation. Most of these gaps can be closed with external UAS documents, and that is what keeps this from "Insufficient." The "percent of the partisan gap explained" figures cannot be regenerated from Table 3 under any single stated baseline.

**Strengths:**

- *Checkable fact:* Full item wording for all 18 topics, 5 reason items and the purpose item is given in Table 2 (p. 5), along with the question stems and response scales (p. 4). This is better than much survey-based education research.
- *Checkable fact:* Table 3 (p. 9) reports N, R², df_m, df_r, F and RMSE for all 14 models, which allows internal checks. For every column, df_r = N − df_m − 1 (e.g., Model 8: 3,892 − 17 − 1 = 3,874). The Model 1 constant (0.47) and Republican coefficient (−1.03) match the Democrat theta mean (0.47) and the 1.03 partisan difference reported on p. 7.
- *Externally verified:* The survey is UAS 567 (fielded September 19 – October 29, 2023). The dates match p. 3. Its data are listed for direct Stata/CSV download on the UAS Education Project page (uasdata.usc.edu), and UAS microdata are available free to registered users with a legitimate research purpose. Figure 1 values I checked match the public topline (e.g., high-school ColorBlind 36.9 + 55.3 = 92; elementary BlkFalseAccus 13.9 + 4.3 = 18; high-school CivWarSlav 47.5 + 26.7 = 74). Table 1's weighted sample proportions (p. 4) match the weighted column of the UAS 567 methodology table.
- *Checkable fact:* The IRT model family (graded response model), the treatment of "I'm not sure" as missing, and the model sequence are stated (p. 6). The paper also states the item-response robustness check (note 2, p. 11) and the omission of state partisanship in Models 9–14 (note 3, p. 11).

**Weaknesses:**

- *Checkable fact:* There is no data availability statement, replication package, code, software/version statement or preregistration (pp. 11–13). The survey is identified only by field dates, never as "UAS 567." The only uasdata.usc.edu citation is for the weighting procedure (p. 13).
- *Checkable fact:* The paper never states whether Figures 1–2 or the Table 3 regressions use survey weights. Only Table 1 is labeled "Weighted." It also never names a standard-error estimator (robust, clustered, design-based). Table 3 reports significance stars but no standard errors or confidence intervals. The UAS 567 methodology notes that multiple respondents per household were not deduplicated, so the lack of any clustering statement matters.
- *Checkable fact:* The sample arithmetic on p. 3 does not reconcile. 3,905/4,896 = 79.8%, not the stated 81%. Table 3 Ns reach 3,973 (Models 2, 4, 6), above the 3,905 "responded." The UAS 567 methodology resolves this: 3,974 invitees (81%) started and 3,905 completed. It also shows that 2,005 and 1,900 are completers classified by self-reported K-12 status, not the sizes of the sampled groups (2,601 and 2,295 were invited). The article's own cited main report (Saavedra et al., 2024, pp. 2–3) gives a third split: 1,763 and 2,142.
- *Checkable fact:* The A/B form design is described only in outline (p. 4). The paper never says which items were paired or which items went on which form. The IRT section (p. 6) does not say how one 18-item scale was built when each respondent saw only 9 items per grade level and the forms share no items.
- *Checkable fact:* IRT reporting is minimal. The paper does not report software, estimation method, theta estimator, item parameters or fit statistics, or whether the calibration used weights. Note 2 (p. 11) cites an AIC/BIC comparison but reports no values. The companion report used a 2PL model in R's mirt package, estimated separately by form (Saavedra et al., 2024, Appendix D, pp. 58–60). The article switches to a GRM without saying whether the by-form estimation was kept.
- *Checkable fact:* The partisanship categories are only partly defined. Thresholds are given only for "strong" states (p. 7). No thresholds are given for leans/purple states or for any county category. No reference categories are stated in Table 3. The "County leans Democrat" row shows 0.00 in all eight columns where it appears, yet df_m for Model 3 is 4. So the row is either an estimated parameter, a displayed base, or a stand-in for a hidden category, and a replicator cannot tell which.
- *Interpretive:* The "share of the gap explained" claims (p. 8; Discussion p. 10) do not state their baseline, and I could not reproduce them from Table 3 (see Detailed Commentary).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- To rebuild the analysis, start from UAS 567 (Stata/CSV at uasdata.usc.edu) and its "Methodology and Topline" document (February 20, 2024 release). That document gives the form assignment, invitee counts and weighting method, none of which appear in the article. Race items rc001/rc002 a–i were on Form A and j–r on Form B. The `form_randomizer` variable identifies each respondent's form.
- The county-partisanship variables (Models 3 and 8–14; Figure A1) require geography finer than state. According to UAS's Restricted Data page, that means an application to the Tier 3 LINKAGE enclave (IRB approval, institutional DUA, outputs vetted before release). Treat those coefficients as unverifiable without enclave access.
- Models 9, 12 and 13 (N ≈ 1,727–1,746) and Models 10–11 (N ≈ 1,784–1,827) use two different random subsamples, while Models 8 and 14 use the full sample. The public topline supports this reading: lm001e–g have Obs ≈ 1,938 and lm001m–n have Obs ≈ 2,003. Note that the methodology document says the "lm" battery was on Form A only, which the Obs counts contradict. Ask for Model 8 re-estimated on each subsample before accepting any "percent explained" figure.
- Treat Figure 2 as low-precision. It reports no Ns or intervals. By my count from 2020 certified results (the paper does not report this), only WY, WV, OK and ND had a Trump share of 65% or more. That is a small population, and each item was seen by roughly half of its respondents.
- Findings that rest entirely on the online appendix could not be checked here because the appendix was not available to me: all subgroup crosstabs and significance shading (Table A1), elementary regressions (A2), midpoint-coding robustness (A3–A4), item-level White-guilt models (A5–A6), the county-level figure (A1) and the theta distributions (A2).

**Detailed Commentary:**

The paper's reproducibility profile has two sides. The substance of the survey is well documented: item wording (Table 2, p. 5), response scales (p. 4) and a consistent set of fit statistics in Table 3. The data also come from a panel whose files are, according to the UAS Education Project page I checked on 2026-09-25, downloadable in Stata and CSV formats for registered users. The descriptive layer holds up when checked against the public topline. Every Figure 1 value I recomputed as agree + strongly agree (with "I'm not sure" left in the denominator, which the Figure 1 note does not state) matched to the point. Table 1 matches the UAS 567 weighted demographics.

The inferential layer is where documentation runs out. For a probability-panel survey, whether the regressions are weighted and how standard errors are computed are first-order specification facts, and the article states neither. The Rao-Scott tests on p. 6 imply design-based crosstabs. Yet the df_r = N − k − 1 pattern in every Table 3 column is what conventional (non-design-based) regression output produces. Weighting with robust variance could produce the same pattern, so I cannot tell which was used. The Table 3 labels (df_m, df_r, RMSE) and note 4's model names ("fullmod," "addwhtgltok") look like Stata output, but no software is stated. The IRT step shapes the dependent variable, and it is described in two sentences plus a footnote equation. A replicator must guess the theta estimator, whether "unsure" responses on the explanatory items were also set to missing, and how the two forms were put on one scale. On the "unsure" question, the Table 3 Ns are consistent with listwise deletion: roughly 1,938 × 0.90 ≈ 1,745 for Model 9. The paper also does not say how the Likert explanatory items were coded; each adds exactly one degree of freedom (df_m 17 → 18).

The most consequential verification problem is the headline decomposition. The text says the White-guilt item "explains more than half" of the partisan gaps, LrnAbtPOCgood explains "approximately 30% to 40%," and LrnAbtPOCbad and TchImpEmbraceDiff "about 25%" each (pp. 8, 10). Using Model 8 as the baseline (Republican −0.94, Neither −0.52), Model 13 reduces the gaps by 49% and 42%. That is not more than half. Using Model 1 as the baseline gives 53% and 51%, but Model 1 has no demographic controls, so the comparison mixes in demographic adjustment. Under the Model 1 baseline, Models 10 and 14 would explain 28–36%, not "about 25%"; under the Model 8 baseline, they explain 19–25%. No single baseline reproduces all four statements. In addition, Models 9–13 are estimated on roughly half the sample, so the coefficient change from Model 8 mixes sample change with attenuation. The Discussion's claim that two items together explain "about half" (p. 10) is never estimated jointly in any reported model. Models 12 and 13 come from the same subsample, so a joint model was feasible.

The sample description should also be read with care. Page 3 describes 2,005 and 1,900 as sampled groups, and 2,005 as "the universe" of K-12 households. The UAS 567 methodology instead describes invitations to K-12 households that had taken part in prior education surveys (UAS559 or UAS479), and gives the 2,005/1,900 split among completers. The same document states that weights were not recalibrated to K-12 household status. The article omits this, even though parental status is a focal comparison. Two smaller wording inconsistencies: the purpose item's 74%/35% split is described as "important or very important" (p. 5), but as "very important" in Saavedra et al. (2024, p. 7). The UAS 567 topline truncates rc001a's label as "An assignment asking students to write about slavery as the main cause of th[e Civil War]," which differs from Table 2's "A history lesson explaining…". Anyone working from the file should check fielded wording against the codebook.

What I searched: UAS survey listings for September–October 2023 (found UAS 567 on the UAS Education Project page); UAS data-access and restricted-data pages; the cited Saavedra et al. (2024) report; and the article title combined with "replication," "OSF" and "preregistration" (no replication package or preregistration found). The UAS Restricted Data page carried a banner saying the repository "is under review for potential modification" per federal directives, which puts long-run access at some risk. Overall, a determined replicator with UAS registration can probably approximate Table 3 and the figures. Only enclave access unlocks the county variables. But the article alone does not let a reader verify how the central RQ3 numbers were produced, and the percentages in the headline claims cannot be reproduced as stated.
